title: Grove separates execution authority from asset custody by routing every external call through the ALM Proxy
content:
Across every integration in A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2 — Aave, Curve, Uniswap V3 — the same two-part shape appears: a controller function performs validation and rate-limit accounting, then executes the actual external interaction via `proxy.doCall(target, abi.encodeCall(...))`.

The proxy is not merely a call forwarder. It is the **holder of record**: Aave deposits credit `aToken` to `address(proxy)` (A...7.1.6), Curve `add_liquidity` mints LP shares to `address(params.proxy)` (A...8.2.6), `remove_liquidity` returns tokens to the proxy (A...8.3.5), and Uniswap positions are "owned by the `proxy`" (A...9.2.5). Approvals are also granted *from* the proxy: `ERC20Lib.approve(proxy, underlying, pool, amount)`.

The separation is what makes the controller replaceable. All policy — which roles may act, which pools are configured, what slippage and rate limits apply — lives in the controller, while the balance sheet lives in the proxy. Upgrading policy therefore does not require migrating assets, and the set of addresses that can ever hold Grove funds stays small and auditable.

The cost is that every operation depends on the proxy's prior state and several steps carry explicit assumptions about it — "assumes the `proxy` has enough underlying" (A...7.1.5), "assumes proxy has adequate aTokens" (A...7.2.3). Those assumptions are not checked, so a mis-sequenced operation fails at the external protocol rather than at Grove's own boundary.
description: The controller validates and rate-limits, then calls proxy.doCall; tokens, aTokens, LP shares and Uniswap positions are all held by the proxy, which is also the recipient of every call.
